final_proof:
Let f_*: P(S₁) → P(S₂) denote the direct-image mapping, so f_*(A) = f[A]. Since the restriction of f_* to τ₁ is a surjection from τ₁ onto τ₂, it is a mapping into τ₂ whose range is all of τ₂. Consequently, τ₂ = {f[U] : U ∈ τ₁}. Call this equality (*).

We first prove that τ₂ is a topology on S₂. Because ∅ and S₁ belong to τ₁, equality (*) gives ∅ = f[∅] ∈ τ₂ and S₂ = f[S₁] ∈ τ₂, where the latter equality uses the surjectivity of f.

Now let (Vᵢ)ᵢ∈I be an arbitrary family of members of τ₂, and for every i put Uᵢ = f⁻¹[Vᵢ], where f⁻¹[Vᵢ] denotes the inverse image of Vᵢ. By (*), for each i there exists Wᵢ ∈ τ₁ such that Vᵢ = f[Wᵢ]. Since f is injective, f⁻¹[f[Wᵢ]] = Wᵢ, so Uᵢ = Wᵢ ∈ τ₁. Therefore ⋃ᵢ∈I Uᵢ ∈ τ₁. Furthermore, the surjectivity of f gives f[f⁻¹[Vᵢ]] = Vᵢ. Since direct images commute with arbitrary unions,

⋃ᵢ∈I Vᵢ = ⋃ᵢ∈I f[Uᵢ] = f[⋃ᵢ∈I Uᵢ] ∈ τ₂

by (*). Thus τ₂ is closed under arbitrary unions.

For finite intersections, take V, W ∈ τ₂ and put U = f⁻¹[V] and Z = f⁻¹[W]. The preceding argument shows that U, Z ∈ τ₁, and bijectivity gives V = f[U] and W = f[Z]. Injectivity of f implies

f[U] ∩ f[Z] = f[U ∩ Z].

Indeed, inclusion from right to left always holds; conversely, if y belongs to the left side, then y = f(u) = f(z) for some u ∈ U and z ∈ Z, so injectivity gives u = z ∈ U ∩ Z. Since U ∩ Z ∈ τ₁, equality (*) now yields V ∩ W = f[U ∩ Z] ∈ τ₂. Closure under binary intersections, together with S₂ ∈ τ₂, implies closure under every finite intersection, including the empty intersection. Hence (S₂, τ₂) is a topological space.

It remains to show that the spaces are homeomorphic. The map f: S₁ → S₂ is bijective by hypothesis. If V ∈ τ₂, the preceding argument gives f⁻¹[V] ∈ τ₁, so f is continuous. Let g = f⁻¹: S₂ → S₁ be the inverse mapping. For every U ∈ τ₁, the inverse image of U under g is g⁻¹[U] = f[U], which belongs to τ₂ by (*). Thus g is continuous. Therefore f is a homeomorphism from (S₁, τ₁) onto (S₂, τ₂), as required.
